title: EFFECTS OF SIGNAGE AND FLOOR PLAN CONFIGURATION ON WAYFINDING ACCURACY
research_question: This study examines the influence of floor plan complexity and several types of signage on wayfinding within a series of buildings on a university campus, specifically: (b) to examine the influence of floor plan complexity on observed wayfinding performance; (c) to investigate the influence of different types of signage on wayfinding performance; and (d) to determine whether there is an interaction between floor plan complexity and the presence and type of signage on wayfinding.

participants.description: 21 females and 34 males, primarily undergraduate students from a university campus. Participants had an average of 3.6 times (SD=1.3) prior experience in the experimental buildings.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five distinct floor plan configurations (Settings 1-5) on a university campus, schematized from existing buildings and manipulated forms. These varied in topological complexity (Inter-Connection Density, ICD) from 1.00 (Setting 1) to 1.75 (Setting 5).

Three signage conditions: no signage, textual signage ('Turn Left Here,' 'Turn Right Here,' 'Destination ahead'), or graphic signage (arrow indicating direction). Signs were 8x16 inch white foam core board, mounted near decision points at 5 ft 6 in height.

measures.instrument: Measured in feet per second by experimenter observation.
Ordinal Likert-type scale (1-5) scored by experimenter observation, defined as retracing a path in the opposite direction.
Ordinal Likert-type scale (1-5) scored by experimenter observation, defined as hesitating or stopping to look at signage or for orientation.
Ordinal Likert-type scale (1-5) scored by experimenter observation, defined as making a turn incongruent with the most efficient path.

mechanisms: Symmetrical forms contain redundant information, making them easier to describe and understand, which can lead to increased confidence and walking speed despite higher topological complexity.
Textual signage provides explicit information, which is highly effective in reducing wayfinding errors like backtracking and wrong turns, though it may take longer to process.
Graphic signage allows for faster processing and higher rates of travel, potentially serving as 'reassurance' signage between major decision points.
Floor plan configuration can have an overriding influence on wayfinding performance, where signage alone cannot fully compensate for problems in highly complex settings.
moderators: Signage type (textual vs. graphic vs. none)
implementation_implications: For facilities where rate of travel is a top priority (e.g., transportation centers), graphic signage might be most appropriate to improve overall flow.

For settings where accuracy and speed are critical (e.g., hospitals, institutional settings, emergency egress), textual signage at key decision points combined with graphic signage for reassurance could be used.
Designers should prioritize simpler floor plan configurations, as signage may not be able to fully compensate for wayfinding problems in extremely complex buildings.

limitations: The study used a noninteractive computer simulation of an imaginary setting, which limited the assessment of actual wayfinding performance (referencing Evans et al. 1984, but implying similar limitations for simulation studies in general, though this study used physical spaces).
The study focused on a specific type of building user (occasional user with some familiarity but novel destination), which may limit generalizability.
The artificial destination prevented reliance on existing signage or architectural cues, which might differ from real-world wayfinding scenarios.
The study did not assess the effects of multiple architectural variables beyond floor plan configuration and signage, acknowledging that other elements like visual access and landmarks also interact.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of Signage and Floor Plan Configuration on Wayfinding Accuracy
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of Signage and Floor Plan Configuration on Wayfinding Accuracy
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Signage is commonly employed to enhance wayfinding efficiency, especially in buildings with complex floor plan configurations. This study examines the influence of floor plan complexity and several types of signage on wayfinding within a series of buildings on a university campus. The study used a 5 x 3 factorial experimental design. The first factor, complexity of floor plan configuration, is defined through five alternatives. The second factor, signage, has three conditions: no signage, textual signage, or graphic signage. The results show that as floor plan complexity increases, wayfinding performance decreases. Graphic signage produced the greatest rate of travel in all settings, but textual signage was the most effective in reducing wayfinding errors, such as wrong turns and backtracking. Overall, the addition of signage resulted in a 13% increase in rate of travel, a 50% decrease in wrong turns, and a 62% decrease in backtracking across the five settings. However, plan configuration was found to exert a significant influence regardless of signage, because the wayfinding performance of participants with access to signage in the most complex settings remained equivalent to, or significantly poorer than, those in the simplest settings with no signage.
